questions.q: What is the programme mainly about?
options: How libraries in Denmark choose which books to buy
Why people are reading fewer books today
How to write a book about your own life
A library where the 'books' are people
questions.why: Neil says it's an unusual library where the books are people who have faced prejudice.

questions.q: What can readers do at the Human Library?
options: Take a person home for a whole day
Have a thirty-minute talk with a 'book'
Read stories written by famous authors
Listen to recordings of people's lives
questions.why: Sam says readers may borrow these 'books' for a thirty minute conversation.

questions.q: Why does the Human Library need to be a safe space?
options: Because the books there are very valuable
Because many visitors are young children
Readers are asked to raise awkward topics
Because meetings take place late at night
questions.why: Readers are encouraged to ask awkward or embarrassing questions, so it needs to be a safe space.

questions.q: According to Ronni Abergel, why do we judge people quickly?
options: We don't have time to get to know everyone
We learn to do it from books and films
Our parents teach us to be careful of strangers
We are usually too shy to talk to new people
questions.why: He says we don't have time on the street to get to know everyone, so 'we drop people in little boxes'.

questions.q: What does Ronni recommend visitors do?
options: Only meet people who are similar to them
Avoid asking any personal questions
Bring a friend to every conversation
Meet people they might feel unsure about
questions.why: He recommends meeting people you might not feel interested in because something makes you uncomfortable.

questions.q: Where does most of the money for the Human Library come from?
options: Donations from the Danish government
Selling tickets to members of the public
Holding events for private companies
Selling books written by its volunteers
questions.why: Neil says money mostly comes from hosting events for private companies, including Google.

questions.q: According to Katy Jon Went, how do people often act around difference at work?
options: They are very careful, afraid of getting it wrong
They ask lots of rude and personal questions
They don't notice any differences at all
They refuse to talk to people who are different
questions.why: She says we're 'walking on eggshells around diversity and difference' because people don't want to get it wrong.

questions.q: What 'incredibly rare offer' does Katy describe?
options: Getting free books from the library to keep
Asking anything without being judged
Meeting famous people from Google
Visiting Human Libraries in 85 countries
questions.why: She says you can ask them anything and they're never going to make you feel wrong for the question.
